scenario_stem:
Northpoint Automation Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago in Country X, producing precision components for packaging machines sold across the region. The business employs 28 technicians yet runs 4 automated pressing lines costing $2.4 million. Annual revenue reached $6.2 million with capital employed of $5.1 million, while a nearby rival employs 210 workers producing assembly parts and reports revenue of $1.8 million.

Northpoint has applied for a government manufacturing award shortlisting the region's largest firms. The entry form asks for size, and the directors must decide whether to claim leadership by number of employees, value of output or capital employed. They are also weighing a $400,000 investment to hire 60 assembly workers against keeping their highly automated operation as it is.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'capital employed'.
questions.model_answer: The total value of the long-term finance invested in a business, equal to non-current assets plus working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) [2].

knowledge_max_2: total value of long-term finance invested in the business
non-current assets plus working capital (or shareholders' equity and long-term liabilities)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the number of people employed may be a misleading measure of business size for Northpoint Automation.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It ignores automation [k], because Northpoint's 28 technicians run 4 pressing lines costing $2.4 million yet produce $6.2 million in revenue while the rival's 210 workers produce just $1.8 million [app]. Reason 2: It ignores capital employed [k], because Northpoint has $5.1 million tied up in assets and pressing lines which the headcount never reveals [app].

knowledge_max_2: number employed ignores productivity / automation
number employed ignores capital / assets invested
application_max_2: $6.2 million revenue vs rival's 210 workers producing $1.8 million
$5.1 million capital employed / $2.4 million pressing lines

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using value of sales to measure business size.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Value of sales says nothing about profit or efficiency [k], because Northpoint reports revenue of $6.2 million but sales figures reveal nothing about what it keeps after costs [app], so two firms with equal sales can differ greatly in financial strength [an]. Limitation 2: It hides production and asset scale [k], because the $2.4 million of pressing lines and $5.1 million of capital employed would never appear in a sales figure [app], so a capital-intensive firm can look small beside a labour-intensive rival [an].

knowledge_max_2: sales value excludes profit / costs
sales value ignores unsold output / assets / capital employed
application_max_2: $6.2 million revenue not the same as profit
$5.1 million capital employed in pressing lines
analysis_max_2: equal-sales firms can differ greatly in financial strength
capital-intensive firms appear small beside labour-intensive rivals

questions.question_text: Do you think Northpoint Automation Ltd should invest $400,000 in hiring 60 assembly workers instead of keeping its automated operation? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in 60 workers would make Northpoint appear larger by the employment measure [k], strengthening its award entry and adding labour capacity it does not currently have [app], which could win larger contracts and push revenue beyond $6.2 million [an]. However, wages would add greatly to costs and reduce productivity [k], because the business's real strength is 28 technicians running $2.4 million of automated pressing lines [app], and 60 extra staff would raise unit costs and slow automated throughput [an]. Overall, Northpoint should keep its automated operation rather than hire 60 workers for appearance [eval], because capital employed, value of output and efficiency are truer indicators of its size than raw headcount [eval].

knowledge_max_2: larger headcount improves ranking on the number-employed measure
extra staff raise wage costs / reduce automation advantage
application_max_2: 28 technicians running $2.4 million of pressing lines
analysis_max_2: bigger headcount may win contracts / award but dilutes productivity

scenario_stem:
Ryecroft Bakeries Ltd is a private limited company founded 7 years ago by Amara Osei in Country X, operating 6 bakeries selling 45,000 loaves a week to households and cafes. The business employs 130 staff, reports annual revenue of $3.4 million and capital employed of $2.1 million. A nearby rival, Hartley & Sons Bakeries, runs 4 bakeries with 85 staff and revenue of $2.2 million, and its owners have offered to merge with Ryecroft, valuing the combined business at $5.8 million.

Amara, Ryecroft's founder, is choosing between accepting Hartley's merger offer or pursuing internal growth instead: opening 2 new bakeries in the south of the city at a cost of $900,000 funded from retained profit. She must weigh faster expansion against losing full control of her family-built brand.

scenario_stem:
Haverstock Furniture Ltd, established 8 years ago in Country X, manufactures wooden office desks and chairs for corporate clients across the region. It employs 40 workers, reports annual revenue of $2.6 million and made a profit of $310,000 last year. Each year it buys 900 cubic metres of oak timber from Suncrest Sawmills at $240 per cubic metre, costing $216,000. The sawmill's owners have offered to sell the business to Haverstock for $1.5 million.

Founder Daniel Whitmore must decide between buying Suncrest Sawmills, a backward vertical integration, to secure the timber supply, or declining and investing $300,000 in a larger showroom to boost sales of finished furniture. He is concerned about managing a sawmill as well as a furniture factory.

Benefit 2: Lower net costs [k], because the $240 per cubic metre paid to Suncrest includes its profit margin, which Haverstock would now capture inside the integrated business [app].

scenario_stem:
Merrow Vale Cider Ltd is a private limited company founded 6 years ago in Country X, pressing apples from 30 local orchards and selling bottled cider to supermarket chains nationwide. It employs 22 staff across picking, pressing and bottling, produces 600,000 bottles a year and sells them at $2.10 each, giving revenue of $1.26 million and profit of $180,000 last year. Supermarkets add a 50-cent mark-up, selling to consumers at $2.60.

Founder Rosa Merrow is deciding between two growth options: opening 2 own shops at $320,000 each to sell direct at $2.60, keeping the 50 cents supermarkets now take; or keeping supermarkets as the main channel and installing a second pressing line costing $500,000 to raise output to 800,000 bottles a year.

questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Higher margin per bottle [k], because selling at $2.60 direct would keep the 50 cents supermarkets currently add on top of the $2.10 paid to Merrow [app]. Advantage 2: Direct customer relationships [k], because own shops would let Merrow build brand loyalty and gather feedback instead of relying on supermarket shelf space [app].

Problem 2: Lack of retailing experience [k], because Merrow knows pressing cider, not running tills, displays and shop staff [app], so poor retail management could leave the shops loss-making and damage the brand [an].

However, the shops cost $640,000 against the $500,000 pressing line [k], and raising output to 800,000 bottles would grow revenue to $1.68 million through proven supermarket channels, while Merrow has no retail experience [app], so slow-selling stock and high running costs could erase the saving [an]. scenario_stem:

Amara wants to expand into 2 new districts. She can either open 2 more cafés costing $110,000 each from retained profit, or buy Bronze Bean Coffee Co, a rival with 3 cafés and 28 staff, for $850,000 using a bank loan. She must decide which route achieves growth without losing control of her brand.

scenario_stem:
Stornaway Appliances Ltd is a private limited company founded 12 years ago in Country X, selling household appliances such as washing machines and refrigerators. It now employs 380 staff across checkout, warehouse and delivery operations, with revenue of $14.5 million, but profit fell from $1.3 million to $700,000. Customer complaints have risen by 40% and absenteeism has also doubled.

The board is deciding whether to continue expanding by acquiring Halcyon Retail, 8 stores with 95 staff, for $2.0 million, or to pause takeovers for 2 years and consolidate: improve training, standardise procedures across stores and rebuild morale and customer service.

Problem 2: Low morale and rising absenteeism [k], because rapid change has doubled absence and squeezed profit from $1.3 million to $700,000 [app], so staff training and standardised procedures should be used to rebuild engagement [an].

scenario_stem:

Revenue per worker at Elmridge is about $60,000; at Halstead it is about $45,000.

scenario_stem:
Briskfield Foods Ltd is a private limited company founded 7 years ago in Country X, producing chilled ready meals such as lasagne, cottage pie and curries sold through supermarkets and convenience stores nationwide. It employs 52 staff and reports annual revenue of $4.7 million with profit of $520,000 last year. Each year it buys 700 tonnes of mixed vegetables from Delmara Farms at $1,100 per tonne, costing $770,000.

Two takeover targets are on offer: Delmara Farms, the vegetable grower, asking $950,000, a backward vertical integration; or Callum Fresh Meals Ltd, a rival ready-meal maker with 30 staff and revenue of $2.3 million, asking $1.1 million, a horizontal integration. Briskfield can afford only one of these two established businesses and must choose.

questions.model_answer: When one business acquires a controlling interest in another business and takes over its assets, operations and management [2].

Advantage 2: Economies of scale [k], because producing more ready meals with shared kitchens, buying and distribution would cut average costs per meal [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Briskfield Foods of buying Delmara Farms instead.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Guaranteed vegetable supply [k], because the 700 tonnes of mixed vegetables Briskfield needs each year would come from its own farm [app], securing uninterrupted ready-meal production through every season [an]. Advantage 2: Capturing the supplier's margin [k], because the $770,000 a year paid at $1,100 per tonne includes Delmara's profit [app], which Briskfield would now keep, boosting its $520,000 profit [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Briskfield Foods Ltd should buy Delmara Farms instead of Callum Fresh Meals Ltd? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying Delmara Farms would secure supply and save money [k]: the $770,000 a year paid at $1,100 per tonne would stay within the enlarged business and Delmara's profit margin would be captured [app], potentially lifting profit well above $520,000 while guaranteeing vegetable supply [an]. However, Callum Fresh Meals offers scale and market share [k]: adding its $2.3 million revenue and 30 staff to Briskfield's $4.7 million would create a near $7.0 million chilled-ready-meal business [app], with shared costs, stronger buying power and fewer rivals [an]. Overall, Briskfield should buy Callum Fresh Meals rather than Delmara Farms [eval], because horizontal integration transforms its competitive position and revenue, while vegetables at $1,100 per tonne are a known market price it can keep buying externally [eval].
